Canada has universal healthcare - but we also pay $1 more per gallon of gas to pay for it - it's a great deal if you don't drive - not so much if you do.

If you drive for a living and buy your own fuel, you are paying through the nose for health care here. Thing is, because you don't see it directly, you don't think of it that way.

We used to pay monthly health insurance fees before y2k - about $18 to $27 per month or so. After they rolled it into the fuel tax - so it's about $15 to $25 in tax in each full tank of gas. About $12 to $20 US at today's exchange rates. It adds up but in a hidden way, and the burden is carried mostly by those wealthy enough to own a vehicle, ie, those wealthy enough to pay for it. Part of the upside is it eliminates 99% of the bureaucracy associated with insurance on the consumer side - you get a health card, and that's it. The paperwork all happens on the doctor's side.

The hospitals themselves are largely run by the doctors. Administration staff are usually also doctors who moved into management. For the most part they are self managing. What they do is too complicated to be managed from the outside anyways. It is a medical technocracy. They are not paid as well as American doctors, and many leave for America in pursuit of higher wages - but they do enjoy an upper middle class lifestyle. It's not like they are hard done by.

Also, there are still all kinds of private medical operators in the system - all of the local clinics, the ambulance services, special clinics such as private MRI facilities, Xray facilities, old folks homes, rehab clinics, etc.... all of which contract with the government and private insurers. Indeed, most of the industry remains privately run, and there is plenty of money being made.

What do we get? Universal coverage regardless of your illness - at a cost approximately 10% of that in America. Not everything is covered in that. Vanity cosmetics are exempt, for example. The system also runs on a triage basis. That means you may have to wait for some services - especially if you are not dying immediately. If you are dying, they won't think twice to spend $1/2 million to save you, with no notice at all. If they can save you, they will.

Canadian companies also enjoy a huge economic advantage in not paying for worker healthcare - (though they are paying higher transportation fees.) This has always been attractive for companies such as the Big three auto makers who ship the bulk of their product back to America by rail. This was offered to the companies after we went with free trade, in part in order to keep these firms here. Prior to free trade, the companies commonly used to pay the health fees for employees.

In the case of long term disability, private insurance still applies - usually offered through the workplace. For the rest, either low value employees, or welfare people - well, they are still on welfare. Disability pays more than basic benefits - but nobody is getting rich on that. You will not starve - but, neither are you forced into a life of crime to survive.

It's comparable to a first world standard... as opposed to a place like Brazil, where people will shoot you in the head to steal the shoes you are wearing. It is far from perfect, there is no doubt of that... but the vast majority of Canadians would never give it up.

One way to look at it is it is not unlike the fire department, or the police - we don't pay directly for those services either - for us, hospital services are the same, another public service - like the guys who run the public utilities.
